title: The Wind in the Willows
author: Kenneth Grahame
openingText: The Mole had been working hard all morning, spring-cleaning his little home. First he used brooms, then dusters; then he climbed up ladders and steps and chairs with a brush and a bucket of whitewash, until his throat and eyes were full of dust, his black fur was spattered with whitewash, and his back ached and his arms were tired out. Spring was stirring in the air above him and in the earth below and all around, and it crept even into his dark, humble little house, bringing a restless, almost holy longing for something more. So it was hardly surprising that he suddenly threw his brush on the floor, said “Bother!” and “Oh, blow!” and then “To blazes with spring-cleaning!” and dashed out of the house without even stopping to grab his coat. Something above was calling him, and he would not be refused. He headed for the steep little tunnel that served him as the gravel driveway owned by animals whose homes are closer to the sun and air. So he scraped and scratched and scrabbled and scrooged, and then he scrooged again and scrabbled and scratched and scraped, working busily with his little paws and muttering to himself, “Up we go! Up we go!” until at last, pop! his snout came out into the sunlight, and he found himself rolling in the warm grass of a great meadow.
about:
Kenneth Grahame (1859–1932) published The Wind in the Willows in 1908. Mole leaves his spring-cleaning for the river, where he meets Rat, who takes him boating and picnicking. The two visit gruff Badger in the Wild Wood and try, again and again, to keep their friend Toad out of trouble as he moves from caravans to motor-cars to prison to a bold return to Toad Hall.

The book is a string of episodes about friendship, home and the pull of the open road. Some chapters are comic, some quiet, and some almost solemn. Songs and poems are scattered through it, and the language is Edwardian; this edition gives it a clear modern rendering.

whyItMatters.title: A book about home and the world outside it
whyItMatters.body: Mole’s burrow, Rat’s riverbank, Badger’s tunnels and Toad Hall each stand for a different way of living. The chapters keep asking whether to stay safe or go out and see more. Readers can compare their own answer with each animal’s.

whyItMatters.title: Friendship tested by a difficult friend
whyItMatters.body: Toad is vain, boastful and reckless, and his friends keep rescuing him anyway. The story asks what loyalty requires when someone will not listen. It is a good book to talk about with a young reader.

whyItMatters.title: An old English river, written with love
whyItMatters.body: Grahame writes about water, seasons and weather in careful detail. The Piper at the Gates of Dawn chapter is quite different in tone from the comic chapters. Reading the two kinds side by side shows how much range a children’s book can have.

angleCards.title: Compare the animals
angleCards.text: Note how Mole, Rat, Badger and Toad each talk, what they want and what they fear.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading The Wind in the Willows to see how each animal is drawn as a character.

angleCards.title: Follow Toad’s adventures
angleCards.text: Track each of Toad’s crazes and how his friends respond to each one.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading The Wind in the Willows to follow Toad’s rise, fall and return.

angleCards.title: Home and away
angleCards.text: Notice each time a character chooses home or the open road, and what it costs.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading The Wind in the Willows to examine the pull between home and adventure.

angleCards.title: Listen to the songs
angleCards.text: Read the songs aloud and note what they add to the scene or the singer’s character.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading The Wind in the Willows to see what the songs and poems add to the story.
